Where it began

Chris Gayle was born in Kingston, Jamaica, on 21 September 1979. His cricket started at the Lucas Cricket Club in the city, and he later gave the club the credit for setting him on his way. Lucas returned the compliment by naming its nursery after him.

He was the West Indies' top scorer at the Under-19 World Cup in 1998, made his first-class debut for Jamaica the same year, and was playing Test cricket by 2000.

The player

Gayle played 103 Tests for the West Indies between 2000 and 2014, making 7,214 runs at 42.19 with 15 hundreds and 37 fifties. He also held 90 catches and captained his side in 20 Tests.

When he got in, he stayed in. Against South Africa in 2005 he batted his side to safety with 317, and in 2010 he made a second triple hundred, joining Don Bradman, Brian Lara and Virender Sehwag as the only men to have done it twice at the time. That second one, 333, was his highest. Against Australia in 2009 he reached a hundred from just 70 balls, and in Dhaka in 2012 he launched the opening delivery of the match over the boundary, a first in Test history.

In the shorter formats he was a force of nature. He made the first century in a Twenty20 international, 117 against South Africa in 2007, and at the 2015 World Cup he hit 215 against Zimbabwe. He was part of the West Indies sides that won the Champions Trophy in 2004 and the World Twenty20 in 2012 and 2016.

What made him special

Gayle was a big man who timed the ball sweetly, and he liked to stand motionless while the bowler ran in, slowing his breathing until he was perfectly balanced. Then the ball would disappear. In an IPL match in 2013 he made 175 not out from 66 balls, with a hundred in 30 of them.

His gentle off-spin brought him 73 Test wickets and a best of five for 34. They came at 42.75 apiece, so bowling was always the hobby and batting the day job.

Away from the middle

In 2015 he set up the Chris Gayle Academy, which uses sport to help young people in Jamaica and the United Kingdom and gives promising cricketers access to good coaching. He published an autobiography, Six Machine, in 2016, and in 2020 began releasing dancehall music. In 2022 Bangalore placed him in their Hall of Fame alongside AB de Villiers.

And finally

He once explained his powerful timing by saying he was very thin as a boy and used a heavy bat. Not every coach would recommend the method. It worked out rather well for him.
